<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - This is a static personal website built with Gatsby (a React-based static site generator) and hosted on Netlify. It pulls markdown content from the `content/` folder, uses GraphQL at build time to generate HTML/CSS/JS assets, then deploys the result to a CDN.

2. File Structure Highlights (Architectural Clues)  
   - **Root config files**: `gatsby-config.js`, `gatsby-node.js`, `.babelrc`, ESLint, Prettier, Husky hooks.  
   - **content/**: Markdown files organized by type (featured, jobs, posts, projects).  
   - **src/**:  
     • `pages/` and `templates/` define page entry points and page-template components.  
     • `components/`: reusable React UI pieces.  
     • `hooks/`, `utils/`: client-side utility code.  
     • `styles/`: theme, global styles, Prism for code highlighting.  
     • `images/`, `static/`: static assets (favicons, PDFs, slides).  
   - **package.json** & **Netlify**: defines build scripts (`gatsby build`, `gatsby serve`) and deployment via Netlify CI.

3. Key Architectural Patterns  
   - **Static Site Generation (SSG)**:  
     • GraphQL schema created at build-time to query markdown and image data.  
     • Gatsby pipelines (`gatsby-node.js`) programmatically create pages from markdown.  
   - **Component-Based UI**:  
     • React components for layout, navigation, sections.  
     • CSS-in-JS (GlobalStyle, theme variables) for styling.  
   - **Content-Driven Structure**: All user-visible content lives in `content/`; code simply transforms and renders it.

4. Main Components and Their Interactions  
   a. **Developer Machine**  
      – Writes code and markdown.  
      – Runs `gatsby develop` or pushes to GitHub (with Husky pre-commit hooks).  
   b. **Version Control / CI**  
      – GitHub hosts the repo.  
      – Netlify watches the main branch, triggers builds on push.  
   c. **Gatsby Build Process**  
      – Reads `gatsby-config.js` plugins and site metadata.  
      – Imports all markdown from `content/` via `gatsby-source-filesystem`.  
      – Transforms markdown to HTML using `gatsby-transformer-remark`.  
      – Exposes data through GraphQL.  
      – Executes `createPages` in `gatsby-node.js` using templates (`src/templates/*.js`).  
      – Bundles React components and CSS into static JS/CSS files.  
   d. **Hosting / CDN**  
      – Netlify deploys the `/public` folder's static assets to a CDN.  
   e. **End Users (Browsers)**  
      – Request HTML/CSS/JS assets via CDN.  
      – Hydrate into a React SPA (for any client-side interactivity).  

5. Diagram Construction Guidelines  
   - **Boxes for each major component**: Developer, GitHub, Netlify CI, Gatsby Build, CDN, Browser.  
   - **Sub-components inside Gatsby Build**:  
     • Content Source (filesystem) → Remark Transformer → GraphQL Layer → Page Templates + React Components → Static Assets.  
   - **Arrows**:  
     • Code & Content → GitHub → Netlify → Gatsby Build → CDN → Browser.  
     • At build: Markdown → Transformer → GraphQL → React → Static files.  
   - **Color/Shape Coding**:  
     • Developer/CI/Hosting as squares.  
     • Build-time data flow (content processing) as a vertical pipeline.  
     • Runtime delivery (CDN → Browser) as a horizontal flow.  

6. Tailoring to a Gatsby-based Static Site  
   - Emphasize the **build-time GraphQL** step that transforms markdown into HTML.  
   - Show **plugins** (filesystem, remark, image processing) as part of the build pipeline.  
   - Highlight **templates** vs **components** distinction: template components map data to pages; UI components assemble layouts.  
   - Illustrate **CI trigger**: Netlify’s webhook on GitHub push → build & deploy.

7. Diagram Elements Checklist  
   - Clear labels: “Gatsby Source Plugins,” “GraphQL Data Layer,” “Page Templates,” “UI Components.”  
   - Directional arrows: show data-flow for both build-time (content → static output) and run-time (CDN → browser).  
   - Color coding: e.g., blue for developer/CI/hosting, green for build-time pipeline, orange for client runtime.

8. Emphasis  
   - Capture all **essential steps**: code push, markdown ingestion, transformation, page creation, static asset generation, CDN delivery.  
   - Don’t over-componentize: focus on logical groupings (Content Source, Transform Layer, Rendering Layer, Deployment).  
   - Use shapes (e.g., cylinders for data, rectangles for processes) and annotate any significant frameworks/libraries (React, GraphQL, Gatsby plugins, Netlify).

By following this structure, your diagram will clearly map how this Gatsby site goes from raw markdown and React code all the way to a live, static website delivered via CDN.
